description: We are building Lunar Landing Site Navigator
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive mission-planning and educational web application that evaluates solar illumination, power generation, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication feasibility across 16 curated lunar landing sites—including NASA’s Artemis III South Pole candidates, CLPS targets, historic Apollo sites, and international missions (2026–2029).

Powered by official NASA LRO LOLA digital elevation models and JPL/NAIF SPICE ephemerides, the platform computes airless lunar horizon profiles, local crater masking, finite solar-disk grazing, solar array orientation trade-offs, and Earth’s libration wobble. It bridges the gap between raw scientific datasets and rapid decision-making through a 360° topographic horizon silhouette, multi-day power and DTE timelines, live countdowns to Sunset and Earthset, side-by-side site and launch-delay comparisons, and an annual landing-window heatmap, alongside dual Mission Planner and Explorer modes.

At the Moon’s South Pole, minor changes in landing coordinates or launch dates can turn continuous sunlight into mission-ending shadow or communication blackouts. Our tool empowers engineers, students, and the public to evaluate trade-offs in seconds.
details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive mission-planning and educational web application that evaluates solar illumination, power generation potential, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio communication feasibility across 16 curated lunar landing sites from 2026 to 2029—including NASA’s 9 updated Artemis III South Pole candidate regions, Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) targets, historic Apollo landing sites, and international lunar missions (Chandrayaan-3 and Chang’e-4).

At build time, our data pipeline ingests NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) 80 m/pixel South Polar Digital Elevation Model (ldem_80s_80m) and topocentric JPL Horizons ephemeris records (MOON_ME frame) for both the Sun and Earth. For every South Pole site, a vectorized geometric raycaster computes 360° topographic horizon elevation profiles across three observer/mast heights (1.5 m rover deck, 2.0 m lander, and 10.0 m solar tower), accounting for lunar spherical curvature and the absence of atmospheric refraction.

At runtime, our physics engine and interactive web cockpit let users:

  • Visualize Sun & Earth vs. the Horizon: View an unwrapped 360° Topographic Horizon Silhouette and polar sky plots showing how local crater rims block or clear the Sun and Earth over time.
  • Assess Power & Communications: Compare three solar array configurations (Horizontal Fixed, Vertical Fixed, and Vertical Sun-Tracking) with finite solar-disk grazing (0.534° solar diameter), track DTE elevation clearance margins, and detect solar conjunction interference.
  • Monitor Operational Countdowns: Read live hours remaining until Sunset/Sunrise and Earthset/Earthrise, longest continuous darkness streaks (critical for thermal and battery survival), and composite Mission Feasibility Scores (0–100).
  • Compare Scenarios & Schedule Shifts: Run side-by-side comparisons of 2–4 sites, simulate launch delays (+14, +29.5, +90, and +180 days), explore a 12-Month Optimal Landing Window Heatmap, and share reproducible scenarios via canonical URL parameters.

What Benefits Does It Have & What Is the Intended Impact?

Existing lunar analysis tools—such as NASA’s QuickMap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons—are powerful specialist systems, but comparing a landing site across shifting dates requires manually extracting and cross-referencing separate topographic and ephemeris datasets.

  • For Mission Planners & Engineers: Accelerates trade-off analysis from hours to seconds when hardware delays or launch slips force teams to evaluate backup dates or alternative sites.
  • For Educators, Students & the Public: Features a dedicated Explorer / Educator Mode alongside Mission Planner Mode, translating selenographic geometry, Earth libration wobble, 29.5-day lunar day/night cycles, and zero-atmosphere lighting into intuitive visual stories.

What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

  • Backend & Data Pipeline: Python 3.12 managed with uv, built on a strict Clean Architecture (Hexagonal Ports & Adapters) separation using FastAPI, Pydantic v2, NumPy, SciPy (map_coordinates bilinear DEM interpolation), HTTPX, PyYAML, Pytest, Ruff, and Mypy.
  • Frontend: TypeScript (strict mode), React 18, Vite, Bun, Zustand (split across mission, 60fps playback, and comparison stores), Three.js, Lucide Icons, custom zero-dependency SVG scientific charts, Vitest, ESLint, and Prettier.
  • Contract & Provenance Integrity: Auto-generated OpenAPI (contracts/openapi.json) and TypeScript schemas (api.generated.ts) from a single Pydantic source of truth, plus SHA-256 manifest verification on all upstream NASA datasets.

How Is Your Project Creative?

  1. 100% Deterministic, Verifiable Physics (Zero Black-Box Hallucination): Rather than guessing mission numbers with generative models, every metric is computed from closed-form spherical trigonometry and verified against JPL Horizons (< 0.05° angular tolerance), with committed site packs enabling instant, network-free offline execution.
  2. Honest Two-Tier Terrain Modeling: South Pole sites (80°S–90°S) use full LOLA DEM raycasting (local_enu East-North-Up tangent alignment), while non-polar comparison sites explicitly report spherical_limb_only geometry—never fabricating elevation or slope data where polar DEM coverage does not apply.
  3. Interactive Engineering Trade-Offs: Users can immediately see why a flat horizontal solar panel yields < 8% power under a grazing 3° South Pole Sun while a 10 m vertical tracking mast achieves > 98% efficiency.

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • No Lunar Atmosphere: Horizon cutoff is governed purely by local terrain ridges and the geometric drop of the lunar sphere without atmospheric refraction or twilight scattering.
  • Finite Solar Disk Grazing: At the South Pole, the Sun moves nearly parallel to mountain ridges; modeling its 0.534° angular diameter captures multi-hour partial-disk grazing transitions.
  • Lunar Libration & Far-Side Constraints: Using the MOON_ME frame captures Earth’s ±7° libration wobble in the lunar sky (explaining periodic Earthsets at polar ridges) and demonstrates why far-side sites like Chang’e-4 have 0% direct-to-Earth visibility.
  • Polar Coordinate Singularities: Resampling DEM patches into a local East-North-Up (local_enu) frame prevents polar stereographic longitude rotation bugs near -90°S.
